### Reviewer 1

The manuscript submitted by Peng et al. concerns the inter-cellular transfer of mitochondria through tunnelling nano-tubes (TNTs), and their application as anti-cancer agents. The mitochondrial transfer field, particularly via TNTs, is an emerging field in cell biology, which has brought about a number of high profile publications relating to their properties, function and exploitation. In spite, of this many questions remain. Therefore, new finding of this hot topic will be very welcome to the TNT and wider mitochondrial community, and thus of interest to the broad readership of Nature Communications.
The paper is very interesting from 2 perspectives. First of all, it provides evidence for a link between mitophagy and TNT conducted mitochondrial transfer. Secondly, the work describes how TNTs could be deployed for the formation of extra-cellular networks for the delivery, and deep penetration, of agents for the purposes of imaging and therapy, such as tumor clearance. These two aspects are both very worthy topics in themselves, but feel very much like two different stories, which might be better suited as different papers. The two parts present very interesting fundamental new knowledge and novel applications, which could in principle be suitable for Nature Communications. However, before publication, either as one paper or two, there are a many concerns that need to be addressed.
A major concern is that the central feature of the paper – inter-cellular mitochondrial transport – has not been irrefutably demonstrated. We really need to see images/ movies of mitochondrial moving fully from one cell to another one. This also goes for other claims, e.g. that mitochondria can move in both directions, and reagents are able to hitch a ride on mitochondria from one cell to another; we need to see this happening. Given the claim of large scale inter-cellular mitochondrial traffic through TNTs this should be achievable.
Other concerns figure-by-figure:
Figure 1
A) Representative panels clearly present very different cell densities. It looks like the TNTs have been quantified by area, with each area containing a different number of cells. So, it might be misleading to state that TNTs are upregulated by siPINK1 treatment. Quantification of N=4 random regions is not really sufficient. Surely, the number of TNTs needs to be quantified per cell over a large number of cells from a suitable number of independent experiments. Furthermore, the assertion in the text that the TNTs span ‘from one cell to another’ is not clear from the images (related to major concern above).
B) In the co-culture it is not clear how the team avoided cross contamination of dyes and siRNAs. Can we be certain the co-localisation is not the result of residual dye/ siRNA carrying over from the cells used to seed the co-culture?
C) The combined red/ green channels make it hard to see red mitochondria within green cell. It would be much better to also show the 2 channels separately.
D) The Y-axis need clarification. What does ‘mitochondrial signalling/ cell area’ mean? The text states that there is an increase in the number of mitochondria and TNTs. The stated increase in mitochondria appears to be on the basis of an increase in mito-tracker intensity, which is not a reasonable assertion. The increase in TNTs needs to be properly quantified (as noted above).
Related to this section of the results we need to see some evidence that PINK1 is knocked down by the siRNA treatment (e.g. by Western blotting).
Figure 2
C) Why is the ‘knock out’ only 30% reduced in PINK1? Shouldn’t it be 100%.
E) Again, quantification is based on random regions of cells, rather than according to the number of cells. What does intensity density mean?
K) Has the Seahorse data been normalised to cell density/ number?
Figure 3
C) Please clarify – have the mitochondria in multiple cells of each type been properly quantified – i.e. more than 1 cell per condition from sufficient biological repeats?
F) Transfer in both directions must be shown (visualised) to claim bidirectionality; see major concern above.
G) Again – have the mitochondria in multiple cells of each type been adequately quantified?
Figure 4
C) Again – Y-axis needs clarification – what does mitochondrial signalling/ cell area mean, and what property does it relate to?
J) What was the purpose of Hoechst in this experiment?
Figure 5
A) Again – quantification is based on random regions of the slide, rather than the number of cells. Comparing A) versus B) – why do the same conditions looks completely different? There are no tubes in the MAD condition in B) but many in A). Cells in the MAD+NIR condition are alive in A) but dead in B)
B) Again, what does intensity density mean?
In summary, the claim that all of the interesting effects onserved are mediated by inter-cellular mitochondrial and reagent transfer through TNT networks needs to be proven by visualisation and robust quantification.

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors constructed the ‘mitochondrial autonomous drive’ (MAD) system, which utilized the down-regulation of mitochondrial autophagy to accelerate mitochondrial intercellular transport and achieve the transportation of exogenous substances for photodynamic therapy of tumors. This provided a new strategy for non-transmembrane drug delivery. The work innovatively utilized mitochondria as drug carriers and achieved deep penetration and delivery of drugs through the tunneling nanotubes (TNTs). Moreover, it was the first to conduct a detailed study on the relationship between mitochondrial autophagy and intercellular transport, and found that inhibiting mitochondrial autophagy could significantly enhance the transport capacity of mitochondria. Overall, this is a well-prepared manuscript. However, there are still several shortcomings. I recommend the acceptance of this work after addressing the following issues.
Major issues:
1. In Fig 2k，FP treatment to knockout PINK1 can enhance the mitochondrial OXPHOS pathway that support the cell-to-cell transfer of mitochondria. Will the increased oxygen consuming lead to tumor hypoxia after FP treatment that limited the photodynamic effect? For this question, experiments that determine tumor oxygen condition is suggested.
2. In Fig 7b, it is intriguing that FP treatment inhibits tumor growth. The authors believe that knocking out PINK1 may increase oxidative stress that works for tumor inhibition. However, in Fig 5b, c, FP treatment shows negligible effects in killing tumor cells or generating ROS. Additional experiments are suggested to address this discrepancy.
3. Tumor tissues consist of various cell types, including immune cells and fibroblasts. Do FP or MAD treatments promote mitochondrial transport between these cells, potentially altering the tumor microenvironment? A recent study (doi: 10.1038/s41586-024-08439-0) reports that mitochondrial transfer from cancer cells to tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes can lead to immune evasion. To address potential concerns that MAD might facilitate tumor immune evasion, additional experiments are needed.
4. The mechanism of mitochondrial autophagy and intercellular transport is very complex. Although the article revealed some mechanisms, many details still need further research. For example, how the inhibition of mitochondrial autophagy specifically affects the formation and function of TNTs still needs in-depth exploration.
5. Further research is needed to study the long-term impact of inhibiting mitochondrial autophagy on cells and the body, as well as the stability and effectiveness of the MAD system in the complex physiological environment of the living body.
6. The article only used the photosensitizer IR780 as a model drug. Whether other types of drugs can also be effectively delivered through this system still needs to be verified. Moreover, there is a lack of comparison with other delivery systems to highlight the advantages of the MAD system in anti-tumor in this study.
Minor issues:
1. It is suggested to add a description of Fig 7a for the schematic illustration.
2. Please check the grammar usage and the format issues in the title and the manuscript. For example, in the title, “for accelerate transport” is suggested to change to “for accelerating transport”.

### Reviewer 3

In the manuscript titled " Leveraging engineered mitochondria through intercellular communication network for accelerate transport and delivery" by Peng et al. the authors investigate a potential drug delivery method based on mitochondrial transportation. Essentially, the authors showed that inhibition of mitophagy can accelerate mitochondrial transportation, which can be exploited as a cargo-system to deliver photosensitizer into the deep internal part of tumors and thus to achieve a better anti-tumor effect.
While the manuscript presents a novel concept, 1)overall the experimental data do not support the conclusions. In addition, 2) the manuscript is poorly assembled in terms of focused concepts, particularly in the abstract and introduction, making at time difficult to follow the rationale. 3) The experiments need additional explanation, and particularly robust experimentation to manipulate mitophagy and mitochondrial transportation (including proteins involved in transport, e.g. Miro, etc), in both gain- and loss-of-function. 4) A major concern of these studies is also how quantitative are these studies, both in cultured cells or tumors, and unclear how this can be manipulated in tumors.
Additional critiques:
1. Downregulated mitophagy enhances mitochondrial intercellular transport via TNTs. The authors claim that mitochondria transport between cells through TNTs by showing that mitochondria staining in a long protrusion structure and assuming that mitochondria is in the process of intercellular transportation. Is there a marker of TNTs? Since the cells look in a very stress shape with lots of long branches, is it possible the long branches containing mitochondria shed off from the cells and engulfed by other cells? How this phenomena is conserved among cell types.
2. Blockade of mitophagy arouses transport driving forces. pX330 backbone plasmid is a not good control. It would be better if the author uses pX330 backbone expressing a non-targeting sequence. The author named the PINK1 knockout group as FP group. All the experiments are using siRNA, other methods to manipulate mitophagy proteins are needed in both gain and loss of function. Also, other proteins involved in mitochondrial transportation including Miro, and other should be tested.
3. The use of IR780 is also problematic. Does IR780 controls mitophagy? what concentrations are localized to the mitochondria. But more importantly, and conceptually, why the compound needs to use the mitochondria intercellular communication to reach different part of the tubules. The existence of TNTs, independently of mitochondrial, should be sufficient for drug diffusion in the tumor.
4. To experimentally test the previous point, the authors should use IR780 analogs that don't localize to the mitochondria, to test their hipothesis.

### Reviewer 4

Here the authors explore the relationship between mitophagy and mitochondrial transport between cells via tunnel nanotubes (TNTs) as a potential avenue for enhancing drug delivery. Mitochondria exhibit complex inter-and-intracellular dynamics, and the authors propose using them as a vector for delivering exogenous treatments. They find that inhibiting mitophagy increases transport of mitochondria (both in number and speed) between cells via TNTs. The authors use the photosensitive drug IR780 to develop a ‘mitochondrial autonomous drive’ system that enhances traffic of mitochondria deeper into tumor tissues to lead to improved outcomes in vitro and in vivo.
My expertise is in advanced light microscopy, so most of my comments concern imaging methodology and interpretation. The cell biology and therapeutic application here seem sound and exciting to me, but there are some flaws in the imaging methodology that need to be corrected for me to have full confidence in the conclusions of those experiments.
The biggest concern for me here is that many of the confocal images included in this analysis are saturated. Saturated images (images with pixel values of 255, in an 8-bit image) are incompatible with quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements. Saturation destroys the mostly-linear relationship between fluorophore density in a specimen and grey values in a digital image. Even a few saturated pixels in a region of interest will disrupt the linearity of the measurement and thus the integrity of the data. There are several instances in this study where saturated images are used for intensity measurements:
Fig 4e. The mitochondria and IR780 channels. In addition to breaking the linearity of intensity measurements, saturation can also cause erroneous dilation of objects and so can confound object-based colocalization analyses as well.
Fig 5b. All of the PI images in the MAD + NIR condition are extremely saturated.
Fig 5c. The DCFHDA images in the MAD + NIR condition
Fig S11. The brightest patches in most of the images are saturated. Pearson’s Correlation is particularly sensitive to saturation because it is impossible to accurately measure how two signals vary relative to one another if one or both of them have hit an upper limit.
I believe that to have full confidence in their image analysis results, the authors will need to re-image the saturated data using appropriate acquisition parameters. Chances are good that most of the major conclusions from these experiments will remain the same (for instance, in Fig 5b and c, saturation may even be causing an underestimation of how much more PI and DCFHDA there is in the MAD + NIR condition relative to the others), but in my experience as a microscopist it is not valid to make quantitative, absolute intensity measurements on saturated data. This is particularly true for sensitive analyses like colocalization and ratiometry.
Additionally bleedthrough controls should be included for most of not all multi-color imaging experiments. A notable example is Fig 4a. One of the conclusions of the figure is that IR780 traffics with mitochondria (labeled with MitoTracker), but signal from the MitoTracker channel bleeding into the IR780 channel would create the appearance of coincidence between the two signals. The authors don’t state which MitoTracker is used in this experiment, but if is MitoTracker Deep Red then bleedthrough is a definite possibility given that there is some overlap between the excitation spectra of MTDR (via FPbase.org) and IR780 (via Fig S9).
An autofluorescence control should be included to demonstrate that mitochondrial/cellular autofluorescence does not change when mitophagy is altered.
The rest of my comments are only minor points.
The image processing and analysis could use a bit more fleshing out, perhaps in the supplementary materials. “ND Processing” is a suite of analysis tools that is exclusive to NIS Elements, and so is not very informative to people who use other types of instruments. Indicating only that analysis was done in ImageJ, LAS, or Zen is not enough information to help people understand how the data was analyzed. How were images pre-processed? (background subtraction, etc)How were ROIs selected? (thresholding? If so, how?) How was particle tracking done?
Avoid displaying images in blue if possible – it is very difficult to see dark blue on a black background.
Overall, the findings here are exciting and significant as a potential avenue for drug delivery, but in my opinion some of the imaging needs to be redone without saturation in order to be analyzed appropriately, and bleedthrough controls should be included in the supplementary material where relevant.

reviewer_updating.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Inspired by the non-transmembrane transfer of mitochondria in cell-to-cell communications, herein, we report an original exploration to accelerate mitochondrial intercellular transport, and its application to exogenous cargo delivery. We discover that deliberate PINK1-targeted mitophagy down-regulation elevates mitochondrial transit capacity via multifaceted drivers—morphological adaptation, metabolic reprogramming, and respiratory enhancement. Capitalizing on this, we engineer high-speed mitochondrial vehicles for photosensitizer hitchhiking, with spatiotemporal tracking elucidating its dynamic intercellular transit and physiological impacts. Through mitochondria’s communication network—tunneling nanotubes (TNTs), the mitochondria-photosensitizer cotransporter achieves reinforced intercellular delivery, thereby inducing deep tumor penetration and enhanced photodynamic killing. Our work establishes a transformative mitochondria-hitchhiking platform for overcoming biological barriers in drug delivery and provides mechanistic insights into manipulating intercellular organelle transport for therapeutic applications.

---

## Introduction

Effective delivery of therapeutics into tumors is the prerequisite for efficient and low-toxic treatment of malignant tumors. However, the abnormal tumor microenvironment—including dense stromal tissue, high interstitial fluid pressure, low blood perfusion, abnormal angiogenesis, and hypoxia—greatly hinders the diffusion distance and extent of therapeutics, forming a ‘blind zone’ in deep tumor where drugs cannot reach1. Currently, multi-functional or ‘smart’ synthetic drug delivery systems aimed at overcoming these obstacles are active and effective, but complex and rigorous, and unable to provide a comprehensive solution to all problems2,3. It has been reported that the delivery efficiency of cancer nanomedicine is less than 1%4, and the limited effect is not conducive to clinical expansion5–7. In contrast, the cell-to-cell transport of substances and signals needed by tumor cells themselves occurs ‘unobstructed’ within tumors. In 2006, Spees et al. first demonstrated that cell-to-cell transfer of mitochondria from mesenchymal stem cells to mitochondria-depleted A549 cells could rescue aerobic respiration8. Studies have shown that mitochondria carry out intercellular transport in a specific manner to improve mitochondrial respiration, restore cell function, and enhance tumor survival9–12. Intercellular mitochondrial transfer depends on biological information communication between donor cells and recipient cells and is mediated by diverse cellular structures, mainly extracellular vesicles (EVs), tunneling nanotubes (TNTs), and gap junctions13. EVs and gap junctions mediate mitochondrial migration between close and adjacent cells, respectively, while TNTs mediate long-distance directional mitochondrial transport14. Rustom et al. first reported TNTs as a new mechanism of intercellular communication in 2004 and termed them ‘Nanotubular highways for intercellular organelle transport'11. Although TNTs are considered to be the major intercellular mitochondrial delivery pathway in solid tumors15–18, the fundamental mechanisms governing TNT-mediated mitochondrial transport remain poor understood.

Changes in cellular energy and metabolism, as well as differences in cell status drive the transport of mitochondria between cells15. Mitochondria precisely regulate themselves through cycles of fusion, fission, biogenesis, mitophagy, and intercellular transport—collectively referred to as ‘mitochondrial dynamics’—to adapt to various physiological states. They frequently alter their morphology or position in response to diverse stressors and energy requirements19,20. However, harnessing mitochondria movement (whether or not carrying cargo) and further enabling it to transport exogenous substances have rarely been explored, highlighting a gap in the understanding of tumor endogenous transport mechanisms that limit their potential to deliver exogenous substances.

Building on these foundations, this study uncovered that suppression of PINK1-mediated mitophagy initiated a compensatory cellular response—engaging cellular homeostatic recalibration and rescue programs. This adaptive rewiring concomitantly potentiated mitochondrial transit velocity/extent through TNTs and mobilized mitophagy-evaded mitochondria as autonomous bio-carriers. Capitalizing on this mechanism, we engineered a ‘mitochondrial autonomous drive’ (MAD) system by spatiotemporally coupling the mitochondria-targeting photodynamic agent IR780 to form ‘passenger-vehicle’ co-transporters. Within solid tumors, MAD orchestrated mitochondrial transport network expansion and high-speed motility through cellular homeostasis and oxidative stress modulation, enabling deep IR780 penetration. Consequently, MAD-mediated photodynamic therapy achieved potent tumor eradication in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, we pioneered a mitophagy-modulated platform leveraging engineered mitochondria for non-transmembrane drug delivery, providing transformative solutions for overcoming penetration barriers in oncology.

---

## Results

Downregulated mitophagy enhances mitochondrial intercellular transport via TNTs
In order to maintain homeostasis, cells undergo autophagy or excretion of mitochondria that have detached from fused filamentous mitochondria during physiological processes. Inhibition of mitophagy may conversely lead to increased mitochondrial transcellular export. PINK1/Parkin pathway is one of the most classic mitophagy pathways, so firstly we verified the effect of the PINK1/Parkin pathway on mitochondrial transport by silencing PINK1.

After 24h culture in the confocal dish, a communication relationship was established between B16F10 cells. Compared with nonsense siRNA control (NC), the fluorescence of mitochondria was significantly enhanced (Fig. 1a), accompanied by a 4.2-fold increase in the number of TNTs, long, thin, membranous structures extending from cells after mitophagy inhibition by siPINK1. Even more fascinating, the images (Fig. 1a) clearly showed that there were mitochondria transferring in the TNTs structure (green mitochondria were present in the red tubular TNT structure). As TNTs are the most important intercellular transport pathway for mitochondria15, the increase in TNTs was closely related to the increase in mitochondrial trafficking.

Afterwards, we designed a donor-recipient cell co-culture system to explore mitochondrial communications between cells after siPINK1 treatment (Fig. 1b). Recipient cells were stained with a living cell tracker CMFDA (green), while the mitochondria of donor cells were stained with MitoTracker (red), respectively. Donor and recipient cells were treated by nonsense siRNA containing medium (abbreviate as NC), or treated by siPINK1 containing medium, respectively. Then, donor cells and recipient cells were co-incubated, and laser scanning confocal microscope (LSCM) was performed to count the number of MitoTracker red spots that were transferred from donor cells in the green recipient cells in four cases, i.e., NC (donor) to NC (recipient), NC (donor) to siPINK1 (recipient), siPINK1 (donor) to NC (recipient) and siPINK1 (donor) to siPINK1 (recipient) (Fig. 1b, c). Images in Fig. 1c showed that almost all green cells contained red mitochondrial signals, indicating that the transfer of mitochondria between cells was ubiquitous. Among them, the red mitochondria of donor cells in recipient cells were significantly increased after siPINK1 treatment (siPINK1 to NC, NC to siPINK1 and siPINK1 to siPINK1) (Fig. 1d). Notably, the mitochondrial transport increased in siPINK1 (donor) to NC (recipient) and NC (donor) to siPINK1 (recipient) may reflect two different mitochondrial transport mechanisms, namely, cells with metabolic changes send dysregulated mitochondria to normal cells to maintain their own quality control, while normal cells transfer healthy mitochondria to unstable cells for rescue21–23. In a separate experiment, conversely, activation of mitophagy using Urolithin A24 resulted in a further reduction in mitochondrial transfer (Supplementary Fig. S1, P<0.0001). This demonstrated that enhanced mitophagy induced compensatory attenuation of the alternative mitochondrial disposal pathway—mitochondrial extrusion—thereby decreasing mitochondrial transfer, in accordance with our hypothesis. Mitochondria traversed between multiple cells (Donor with Donor, Donor with Recipient, Recipient with Recipient cells, respectively) to form a network through TNTs (Fig. 1e), and TNTs acted as a communication bridge between donor and recipient cells, as observed from 3D confocal microscopy image (Fig. 1f). These results highlighted that inhibiting mitophagy enhanced mitochondrial transfer by increasing the number of mitochondria and TNTs.

Blockade of mitophagy arouses transport driving forces
The above research suggests that blockade of mitophagy in the tumor opens up the extensive TNTs transport channels. Replacing siRNA with CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing to knockout PINK1 could modify the short-term inhibition and unpredictable off-target effects of siRNA25,26. The sgRNA targeting PINK1 gene was cloned into pX330 backbone to construct a CRISPR/Cas9 gene knockout plasmid. Then the plasmid was combined with cationic polymer fluorinated highly branched poly(β-amino ester) to form the plasmid delivery nanocomplex27,28 (named FP, the detail were presented in Supplementary Methods and Results and Supplementary Tables 1–2). As a result, the gene editing efficiency was as high as 41.6% after treatment with this CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system (Fig. 2a, b), with a weak expression in PINK1 protein (about 35.7% reduction) compared with the negative control plasmid (Fig. 2c). Taken together, this CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system could induce indels at the targeted PINK1 loci (Supplementary Figs. S2–7) and thus efficiently disrupt the expression of PINK1. The Keima and mitochondria co-localization marker plasmid (mKeima-Red-Mito-7)29,30 was performed to evaluate mitophagy after PINK1 gene editing (Fig. 2d). In Fig. 2e, the red/green fluorescence signal ratio (indicating the proportion of mitochondria under acidic conditions) decreased by 51.8% after CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system treatment in B16F10 cells, revealing the inhibition of mitophagy.

RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of cells transfected with PINK1 plasmid revealed 2457 upregulated genes and 1699 downregulated genes (including PINK1, Fig. 2f). KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed that descending genes were strongly correlated with glycolysis and mitophagy (Fig. 2g). The biological process analysis in GO functional enrichment analysis showed that the transcription-related capabilities were decreased (Fig. 2h). Further analysis of the differentially expressed genes found that genes related to transcription and translation were downregulated, which may be related to the DNA mismatch caused by CRISPR/Cas9 system and the subsequent decrease in PINK1 transcription and translation. The decrease in mRNA related to glycolysis may indicate an increase in aerobic respiration caused by an increase in mitochondria (Fig. 2i). Protein interaction network analysis revealed that the reduced mitophagy-related genes formed a network relationship centered on PINK1 (Fig. 2j), which also underlined the rationality of our inhibition of mitophagy by knocking out PINK1.

Mitochondria are the energy source of cells, and mitochondrial dynamics are closely related to the energy supply within cells31. Mitochondria respiratory capacity reflects metabolic function. To verify that PINK1 knockout improved cell metabolism, respiratory capacity of mitochondria was investigated. Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was recorded to monitor oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) in real time, and inhibitors of mitochondrial respiration were added successively: oligomycin, which inhibits ATP production in mitochondria; FCCP, an ionophore that uncouples mitochondrial respiration leading to maximal oxygen consumption; and antimycin A & rotenone, inhibitors of electron transport complexes I and III, respectively, which completely block mitochondrial OXPHOS. As Fig. 2k showed, the entire OCR curve was elevated after PINK1 gene editing treatment, but still maintained the same sawtooth shape as the control group. According to statistics, the basal respiration, maximum respiration, and spare respiration capacity of cells were significantly improved by PINK1 blockade (2.1-, 4.1-, 5.0-fold versus control), showing a stronger metabolic activity without inducing hypoxia (Supplementary Fig. S8). Increased cellular metabolism is a powerful driving force behind mitochondrial intercellular transport15,32. This suggested that PINK1 knockout can globally enhance the mitochondrial OXPHOS pathway, and the enhanced metabolic phenotype supported the cell-to-cell transfer of mitochondria.

Inhibition of mitophagy increases mitochondrial motility and bidirectional transport
Mitochondrial morphology and motility at the subcellular level provide more direct visualization of their movement dynamics and behavioral tendencies. From the 3D imaging and reconstruction of mitochondria by structured illumination microscopy (SIM), we found that knockout of PINK1 increased the round mitochondria (the aspect ratio of each mitochondrion in 1.0≤L/W<1.5), and decreased the tubular mitochondria (the aspect ratio of each mitochondrion in 2.0≤L/W<5.0) (Fig. 3a). As we know, mitochondria can fuse or fission from the mitochondrial network as the cell state changes. Mitochondrial fission produces individual mitochondria that are more suitable for transport along the actin or microtubule network33, so the small round, more freely and quickly moving mitochondria that shed from the mitochondrial network may have the potential to be used to increase mitochondrial transport.

Previous experiments have shown that decreased PINK1 expression can induce increased mitochondrial migration along TNTs (Fig. 1). Given the increased transport driving forces (Fig. 2), we speculate that the moving speed of mitochondria increases. So, in the following, we explored the speed and pattern of mitochondrial movements within and between cells (in TNTs) under different treatments, respectively.

Continuous imaging for 3 min at 5 s intervals with SIM and tracking of mitochondrial trajectories (Supplementary Movies 1 and 2) were performed to study the alterations on mitochondrial motility in individual cells. The speed-position diagram of mitochondria migration paths in the cytosol (Fig. 3b) and the displacements normalized into the X–Y coordinates (Fig. 3c) underlined that the number of high-speed mitochondria increased, as well as the mean track speed (1.3-fold versus control) and track length (1.7-fold versus control) increased under the blockade of PINK1.

Next, we conducted an in-depth and intuitive visualization study on the movement of mitochondria between cells via TNTs. First, mitochondria and TNTs (F-actin) were marked with pAcGFP1-Mito and LifeAct-mCherry plasmid, respectively, and long-term SIM images of a fixed field of view for up to 20 min were captured (Supplementary Movies 3 and 4). The movement of mitochondria along TNTs was rendered and tracked (Fig. 3d, e), visually demonstrating that the treated mitochondria were generally faster in cell-to-cell transfer, with more high-speed mitochondria shuttling through TNTs. Similarly, mitochondria in cells with PINK1 knockout had faster trajectories (2.0-fold versus control) and longer displacements (1.6-fold versus control) in TNTs when both directions normalized to X-Y coordinates (Fig. 3e), reflecting their enhanced motility. Ultimately, long-term imaging captured complete visuals of a mitochondrion transporting from one cell to another in the FP group, which directly proved the intercellular transfer of mitochondria (Supplementary Fig. S9, Supplementary Movie 5).

Then we labeled the mitochondria of PINK1 knockout and untreated cells with green and red, respectively, and co-cultured them to observe the mitochondrial movement pattern between the two individual cells connected with TNT. The results intuitively showed that the exchange of mitochondria between the two cells was mutual (Fig. 3f, and Supplementary Movie 6), which was consistent with our previous explanation of the bidirectional mitochondrial transport mechanism, the ‘maintaining homeostasis’ and ‘rescue’. Excitingly, the movement trajectories of the PINK1 knockout cells were faster (1.3-fold versus control) and longer (1.8-fold versus control) than those of untreated cells (Fig. 3g), which may indicate that mitochondria in cells with reduced PINK1 expression are more inclined to move between cells and transfer from donor cells to recipient cells.

Cargo IR780 hitches a ride on mitochondria for efficient transport along TNTs
Based on the previous studies that decrease in mitophagy induced an increase in mitochondrial cell-to-cell transport, we designed and constructed a ‘mitochondrial autonomous drive’ (MAD) system, containing FP and FIS (integrating SPION and IR780) nanoparticles, to exploit accelerated mitochondrial motility for cargo delivery. Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle (SPION) is an excellent but short-lived oxidative stress generator at subtoxic concentrations34. Skillfully, when SPION was applied under low-mitophagy condition, as the significantly increased DCFH-DA-stained ROS displayed (Supplementary Fig. S10), the oxidative stress was effectively accumulated to provide more sufficient and long-lasting fuel for mitochondria movements, which was not achieved by SPION alone. IR780 has a natural property of attaching to mitochondria, which is attributed to its highly electropositive and lipophilic nature35, and has been widely used in medical fields such as mitochondrial imaging36 and photodynamic tumor therapy37. So IR780 was selected as a model cargo for delivery, in the form of nanoparticles.

The nanoparticle containing SPION and IR780 (named FIS) was prepared with ∼80 nm diameter and ∼50 mV zeta potential (Supplementary Figs. S11–13, the detail in preparation and characteristics of FIS was presented in Supplementary Methods and Results). IR780 exhibited much higher overlay with mitochondria than lysosomes in the B16F10 cells according to Pearson’s coefficients analysis (Supplementary Fig. S14), emphasizing that the IR780 in MAD was highly accumulated in mitochondria.

MAD treatment increased mitochondrial superoxide (19.3-fold versus control, Fig. 4a) and mitochondrial calcium flux (3.8-fold versus control, Fig. 4b), higher than the group treated with FP alone, highlighting MAD created and maintained a stronger oxidative stress environment for mitochondria migration.

The transfer capacity of mitochondria (red fluorescence) and hitchhiker IR780 (magenta fluorescence) from donor cells to recipient cells was investigated employing the donor-recipient system described previously (Fig. 1b). FIS alone served as control. Mitochondrial migration was enhanced when MAD-treated cells served as donor cells (MAD to FIS, MAD to MAD) (Fig. 4c), which was consistent with previous findings (Fig. 1c, d). Excitingly, IR780’s migration was simultaneously enhanced, and the groups of MAD treated donor cells showed the strongest migration of IR780 hitchhiking on mitochondria, exhibiting a stronger outward transport capacity. Conversely, as demonstrated in Supplementary Fig. S15, recipient cells cultured in conditioned medium exhibited no detectable MitoTracker or IR780 staining, indicating that the fluorescent signals in recipient cells can be attributed to mitochondrial transfer rather than dye crossover contamination. Typical pharmacological inhibitors—cytochalasin D (restraining actin polymerization and thus TNT formation38), L-778123 (inhibiting farnesyltransferase and geranylgeranyltransferase type 1 related to nanotube-mediated intercellular communication39) and dynasore (a non-competitive GTPase inhibitor40) blocked the transfer of mitochondria and IR780 from donor cells to recipient cells (Fig. 4d, P<0.0001 compared with MAD group). These results emphasized that under the driving forces caused by MAD system, shed mitochondria employed TNTs to radiate to surrounding cells under the purpose of maintaining homeostasis, and cargo IR780 followed to migrate to other cells; at the same time, rescue signals were sent to obtain mitochondria and IR780 from other healthy cells.

Further, we showed the synchronous movement of mitochondria and IR780. Through 20 min long confocal fluorescence imaging (Supplementary Movie 7), we observed that IR780 and mitochondria were transported together along TNTs (Fig. 4e), representing that IR780 can hitchhike on mitochondria to transfer from one cell to another without crossing membrane. The 3D rendering of mitochondria and IR780 moving in TNTs (Fig. 4f) clearly revealed the spatial positional relationship among TNTs, mitochondria, and IR780, indicating that IR780 and mitochondria shuttled synchronously inside the TNTs formed between cells in a mutually fused manner.

To demonstrate MAD’s versatility in delivery, we used 10-N-nonylacridine orange bromide (NAO), which employed ΔΨm-independent cardiolipin-specific binding41. NAO showed excellent mitochondrial colocalization (PC=0.90, Supplementary Fig. S16a) and transmission efficiency comparable to IR780 (Supplementary Fig. S16b), confirming MAD’s broad applicability. Virtually any attachable molecule/peptide—through linkage to triphenylphosphonium (TPP) or mitochondrial targeting peptides (MTP)—could be mitochondria-targeted using our MAD system. In contrast, ICG (hydrophilic/sulfonated) and IR780 (lipophilic/ammonium-iodide) shared heptamethine NIR cores but diverged in localization: IR780 showed mitochondrial accumulation (PC=0.83) versus ICG’s diffuse distribution (PC=0.08). Correspondingly, ICG exhibited minimal transfer in MAD (Supplementary Fig. S16b), confirming that mitochondrial loading was essential for intercellular delivery.

Key molecules mediating mitochondrial transport along TNTs deliver a reliable, direct window into the mitochondrion-dependent transport behavior of cargo IR780 within cells. M-sec (TNFAIP2) protein functions as a key regulator of membrane nanotube formation by interacting with the Ral-exocyst pathway42. Knockdown of M-sec protein expression by M-sec siRNA suppressed TNT formation, leading to a decrease in both IR780 and mitochondria trafficking (Fig. 4g). M-sec was found colocalized with F-actin, while IR780 colocalized with mitochondria (Fig. 4h) in MAD treated cells. These results suggested that the intercellular transmission of IR780, like mitochondria, depends on the formation of intercellular TNTs.

MAD controls the switch of cell death though NIR
The previous results have verified that MAD can deliver appropriate cargo (IR780) by leveraging mitochondria in tumor. Based on the important role of TNTs in mitochondrial intercellular transmission as above indicated, we focused on the effects of MAD on TNTs. Confocal images showed that TNT counts slightly increased after FP treatment (2.8-fold versus control), and significantly increased after processing with MAD system (13.5-fold versus control) to form a bundle of interconnected networks (Fig. 5a). This phenomenon was very prominent and also emphasized the importance of SPION in MAD system to produce diverse, long-term driving forces for mitochondrial transport.

In addition, since IR780 is an excellent photosensitizer, we used near-infrared light (NIR) to irradiate MAD treated cells (808 nm, 1 W/cm2 for 20 s) and found that TNTs disappeared almost completely (Fig. 5a), and the tumor cells were dead (Fig. 5b). In fact, NIR aroused a lethal photodynamic effect (7377.7-fold versus control, Fig. 5b), as well as an explosive increase in ROS (4775.2-fold versus control. Fig. 5c), highlighting the extensive distribution and phototherapy efficacy of IR780 in the tumor.

As a contrast, without NIR irradiation, ROS levels increased slightly (1.0% of NIR given) and the cells survived (no significant difference from control). Notably, the cell mortality rate was more than 10,000 times higher upon the NIR irradiation than that without NIR irradiation, greatly highlighting the safety of MAD and the effectiveness of the photodynamic therapy. In addition, it cannot be ignored that the complete MAD system without NIR resulted in 49.5-fold more ROS production than the control group but almost no cell death, which supported the concept of activating mitochondrial intercellular transport by causing cellular oxidative stress without affecting their survival. We anticipated that MAD with NIR would lead to better phototherapy effects, and meanwhile destroy the rescue road of mitochondria transferring, bringing a ‘utilize first and then eliminate’ effect.

IR780 achieves deep penetration through TNTs in tumor
Deep and widespread penetration into tumor is a prerequisite for high efficiency and low toxicity of cancer drugs. Based on previous results, we speculated that intercellular transport by piggybacking on mitochondria could bypass the physical barrier and reach deeper tumor sites. So, B16F10 tumor spheroids were constructed to detect the penetration of IR780 in MAD. The IR780 fluorescence in the tumor spheroids was scanned layer by layer with laser confocal scanning from bottom to top. As the slice section came to the middle, the fluorescence of IR780 in MAD became much higher than that of FIS along (Fig. 6a), revealing greater tumor penetration and accumulation of IR780 in whole tumor. The B16F10-bearing tumor mice model was constructed to examine the tumor penetration ability of MAD in vivo (Fig. 6b). Whether at the border or the core of isolated tumor, the fluorescence intensity of IR780 after MAD treatment was significantly higher than that of FIS alone (Fig. 6c). At the same time, we observed strong overlap of IR780 and TNT structures connecting two cells in tumor sections, highlighting that IR780 diffused through TNTs (Fig. 6d). These results indicated that IR780 can achieve excellent penetration when carried on mitochondria through TNTs, which also laid the foundation for the MAD system to achieve better therapeutic effects in vivo.

MAD system enhances anti-tumor effects in vivo
Cancer photodynamic therapy has been widely used in medicine due to their unique advantages such as minimal invasiveness, potential for tumor ablation, and few side effects44. Next, we verified whether this MAD system could enable the photodynamic therapy drug to achieve better therapeutic effects in vivo. B16F10 melanoma cells were implanted into the right flank of immunocompetent C57BL/6J mice. Animals were randomized into six treatment groups, and different preparations were administered peritumorally, as shown in Fig. 7a. The tumors in group ① (control) grew rapidly (Fig. 7b, c, Supplementary Fig. S17). In groups ② (FP), ③ (FIS+NIR(+)) and ④ (MAD+NIR(+)), the growth rate of tumors declined compared with control, indicating that knocking out PINK1 or SPION/IR780 may exert their effects by accumulating oxidative stress damage of tumors (Supplementary Fig. S18). Group ⑥ (MAD+NIR(++)) that received three treatment cycles produced a significantly reduced tumor growth, and three out of seven animals had complete tumor regression (Fig. 7d), highlighting photodynamic therapy drug can achieve tumor destruction by hitchhiking on mitochondria in MAD system plus NIR. During these treatments, no significant changes were observed in mouse body weight (Fig. 7e). H&E staining of major organs (Supplementary Fig. S19), sequencing of target gene loci in major organs (Supplementary Fig. S20), and blood routine parameters (Supplementary Fig. S21) showed no abnormalities, indicating the safety of MAD system. H&E staining, Ki67 staining, and TUNEL assay of tumors (Fig. 7f–h) showed that MAD under NIR irradiation had the best tumor proliferation inhibition and cell apoptosis ability, concomitant with a tendency toward CD8+ T cell activation (Supplementary Fig. S22).

Following, we sought to dissect the reasons for the different therapeutic effects of these regimens, with a particular focus on the mechanistic changes in vivo associated with mitochondrial trafficking. Compared with control, immunofluorescence results of all treatment groups showed that both M-sec and Miro-1 proteins increased in the tumor tissue (Fig. 7i, j), indicating an increase in TNTs and an increase in mitochondrial movement along TNTs. In Supplementary Fig. S23, additional tumor immunofluorescence analyses revealed upregulated KIF5B (microtubule motor for mitochondrial anterograde transport45) and MYO19 (mitochondrial-specific myosin regulator46), confirming coordinated enhancement of mitochondrial trafficking machinery.

After treatment with PINK1 plasmid in group ② (FP), the protein expression of PINK1 decreased further after each administration cycle (Fig. 7k). And in Fig. 7l, the reduction of PINK1 in group ② and ④ inhibited the phosphorylation of Parkin, further inhibited the conversion of LC3-I to LC3-Ⅱ, and reduced the consumption of the substrate p62, whereas this mitophagy process (Fig. 7m) did not change in the absence of FP treatment (group ① and ③). It should be noted that only the PINK1/Parkin pathway is the main pathway of mitophagy19, while the LC3-I/Ⅱ and p62 pathways are common to all autophagy47, and p62 is also related to the apoptosis signaling pathway48, so their changes were not as typical as Parkin phosphorylation. For example, the higher level of p62 in group ③ than in group ② may be related to apoptosis caused by phototherapy. These results highlighted the changes in mitophagy-related pathways in tumors. MAD inhibited the mitophagy pathway49 (Fig. 7m), especially inhibited PINK1 expression and the downstream Parkin phosphorylation, thereby causing MAD to break the homeostasis of cells and promote the movement of cargo in mitochondria between cells to reach the inside of tumor to exert its effects.

Animals
Female C57BL/6J mice (6–8 weeks) were purchased from Department of Animal Science of Peking University Health Science Center. All animals were acclimated to the facility for one week before experimentation and housed under a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle, at a controlled ambient temperature of 25 ± 1 °C and 55 ± 15% humidity in specified pathogen free (SPF) conditions. Only female mice were used in this study to control for hormonal variability. For technical procedures (e.g., subcutaneous injection), animals were briefly restrained using a soft, non-invasive rodent restrainer. Every effort was made to perform procedures swiftly and calmly to minimize the duration of restraint. Animals were monitored daily for signs of pain, distress, or illness, including but not limited to posture, activity levels, food and water intake, and any visible abnormalities. At the end of the experiment, mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation under anesthesia. All animal experiments were performed strictly with the protocols stipulated by the Guideline for Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of Peking University Health Science Center and approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Peking University Health Science Center (assigned number: LA2022340 and PUIRB-LA2023263).

Cell culture
B16F10 melanoma cells were originated from American Type Culture Collection and were cultured in DMEM medium with FBS (10%), penicillin (100 U/mL) and streptomycin (0.1 mg/mL). All cells were maintained in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO2.

Donor cells and recipient cells system
B16F10 cells (2×105 cells/mL) were seeded and divided into two experimental groups: donor cells (D) and recipient cells (R). siPINK1 (50 nM)/FP (Plasmid: 1 µg/mL) were given in D-siPINK1/FP and R-siPINK1/FP group for 48 h or 72 h, respectively. Then the donor cells were treated with FIS (3.0 µg/mL for IR780) for 4 h and labeled by MitoTracker and Hoechst 33342, while recipient cells were stained with CMFDA and Hoechst 33342. Donor cells were transferred and co-incubated with recipient cells for 4 h. Laser scanning confocal microscope (LAS X 3.7, LSCM, TCS SP8 STED, Leica, Germany) was performed to observe the intercellular communication between donor and recipient cells. Recipient cells were segmented using Cellpose (https://www.cellpose.org), followed by processing of the resultant masks in ImageJ (1.54f) to define cellular boundaries. Individual recipient cells were isolated by subtracting these masks from raw images. Subsequent ‘Analyze Particles’ analysis (with size thresholding and ‘Add to Manager’ enabled) generated discrete regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to individual cells. Mitochondrial and IR780 fluorescence channels were then imported, converted to 8-bit, thresholded at a fixed value across all experimental groups, and converted to binary single-point representations. These puncta were normalized to unity (=1) using the Divide function, enabling quantification via the Measure tool which recorded RawIntDen values—representing the summed intensity of all pixels within each recipient cell ROI—to determine counts of mitochondrial and IR780 puncta per cell. During quantification, RawIntDen values were normalized against recipient cell area to account for size-dependent variability, thereby yielding mitochondrial/IR780 puncta density per cell as the definitive metric for cargo delivery efficiency to recipient cells.

For inhibition experiments, donor and recipient cells were cultured respectively in DMEM with FP containing different inhibitors, cytochalasin D (0.5 µM), L-778123 (10 µM) and dynasore (80 µM) for 24 h. Then donor and recipient cells were treated with FIS and stained as the same steps as above, and co-incubated in DMEM with inhibitors for 4 h, respectively, followed by imaging.

For M-sec and Miro-1 knockdown experiments, donor and recipient cells were cultured respectively in DMEM with FP, and siM-sec/siMiro-1 (100 nM) were transfected into both cells via PEI 25k for 48 h. Then donor and recipient cells were treated with FIS and stained as the same steps as above, followed by imaging.

Bleed through control for MitoTracker Deep Red and IR780, and cellular autofluorescence control following mitophagy modulation, are provided in Supplementary Figs. S24 and S25, respectively.

Western blot for protein detection
B16F10 cells were lysed with RIPA lysis buffer (including PMSF) and protein concentration was unified with Enhanced BCA Protein Assay Kit. The protein samples were boiled, separated by SDS-PAGE gel electrophoresis and transferred with PVDF membrane. Next, membrane was blocked with 5% skim milk (5% BSA for phosphorylated proteins), and then primary antibody and secondary antibody were incubated in sequence. Finally, Immobilon Western HRP Substrate (Millipore, USA) was added and a gel image processing system (Amersham Imager 600, GE, USA) was used to analyze the gray value of the target band. Protein expression was quantified as the intensity ratio of target protein bands relative to loading control bands. Complete uncropped western blot data were shown in Supplementary Figs. S26–29.

Structure illumination microscopy (SIM) for super-resolution fluorescent imaging
To analyze mitochondrial morphology, Multi-SIM system (NanoInsights-Tech) with a Nikon ×100, 1.49-NA oil objective and imaging system were used for 3D-SIM imaging. After FP treated for 72 h and pAcGFP1-Mito transfected for 48 h, cells were seeded onto confocal glass-bottomed dishes 18–24 h prior to imaging. 3D-SIM images were acquired with 488 nm laser. Z-stack performance was set as 0.27 µm/slice per field. Cells were maintained in 37 °C and 5% CO2 during imaging. Multi-SIM images were analyzed using ImageJ. Following threshold optimization, shape descriptors were enabled in ‘Set Measurements’ (with Limit to threshold selected). ‘Analyze Particles’ was then executed, with the Aspect Ratio (‘AR’) column recording the major/minor axis ratio (‘L/W’) as a metric of morphological elongation.

To observe real-time mitochondrial movement, Polar-SIM system (AiryTechnology) with a Nikon ×100, 1.49-NA oil objective and imaging system were used for 2D-SIM imaging. After FP treated for 72 h and pAcGFP1-Mito/LifeAct-mCherry/pDsRed2-Mito transfected for 48 h, cells were seeded onto confocal glass-bottomed dishes 18–24 h prior to imaging. 2D-SIM images were acquired with 488 nm and 561 nm laser for 36 loops in movement within cells and 120/ 30 loops for movement between cells. Cells were maintained in 37 °C and 5% CO2 during imaging. ND processing in NIS-Elements (Nikon, Japan) was used to correct the jitter of long-term images. Polar-SIM images were analyzed by Imaris software (9.0.0). Surface rendering of mitochondria was generated in consecutive images. Tracking project was used to depict traces of single mitochondrion. Through autoregressive algorithm, tracks with >10 s duration for movement within cells and >20 s duration for movement between cells were analyzed and dynamic parameters were calculated. Quantitative motility parameters—‘Track Speed Mean’ and ‘Track Displacement Length’—were acquired in Imaris (‘Statistics’ panel) and subjected to statistical analysis. Cellular metabolic assays
Cellular OXPHOS were assessed with Seahorse XF Pro extracellular flux analyzer (Agilent Technologies, USA). Briefly, B16F10 cells were cultured as 2×104 cells/well in a XFe96 cell culture microplate. Prior to metabolic measurements, supernatant was removed and replaced with Seahorse assay medium. The cells were then incubated in a CO2-free incubator for 1 h. Oligomycin (1.5 µM), FCCP (1.5 µM), and R&A (0.5 µM) were injected sequentially. Finally, Hoechst 33342 reagent was injected to quantify the cell number using a high-content analyzer (CellVoyager CV8000, Japan) for normalization. The parameters in the assay were analyzed in Seahorse Analytics (Agilent Technologies, USA).

Flow cytometry for in vitro detection
Cells suspension was prepared in PBS after incubating. For samples that required staining, DCFH-DA (10 µM), MitoSOX (5 µM) or Rhod-2 (5 µM) were added to the cells for 20 min, followed by washing with PBS and passing through a 200-mesh cell sieve. Samples were examined using Cytoflex flow cytometer (CytExpert 2.5, Beckman Coulter, USA). All data were processed using FlowJo software (V10). Details of the gating strategy were provided in Supplementary Figs. S30–33. Typically, 10,000 live cell-gated events were acquired for analysis.

RNA-seq for gene expression
RNA sequencing and analysis were performed by Novogene. Specifically, sequencing libraries were generated using NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB, USA) following manufacturer’s recommendations and index codes were added to attribute sequences to each sample. The raw data were filtered to obtain clean data, and Q20, Q30 and GC content of the clean data were calculated. The reference genome was indexed using HISAT2 v2.0.5, and paired-end clean reads were aligned to the reference genome using HISAT2 v2.0.5. FeatureCounts (1.5.0-p3) was used to count the number of reads mapped to each gene. The FPKM of each gene was then calculated based on the length of the gene and the number of reads mapped to the gene. Differential expression analysis between two comparison combinations was performed using edgeR (3.22.5). Genes with FDR <0.05 and absolute log2 fold change >1 were identified as differentially expressed genes. The DAVID database (https://david.ncifcrf.gov) was used to analyze the GO and KEGG datasets. The STRING database (http://string-db.org) was used for functional protein association network analysis of differentially expressed genes.

Intracellular ROS detection
B16F10 cells (2×105 cells/mL) were seeded and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Then the cells were incubated with FP for 72 h and FIS for 4 h, respectively. Then untreated cells were used as control. Then, DCFH-DA (10 µM) was added at 37 °C for 20 min, and the cells were irradiated (808 nm, 1.0 W/cm2, 20 s) after washing. Finally, cell nuclei were stained with Hoechst 33342 (5 µg/mL) and observed by CLSM (ZEN 3.9, LSM880, Zeiss, Germany). All images were processed in ImageJ following a standardized workflow: raw data underwent 8-bit conversion followed by application of identical channel-specific thresholds across experimental groups before intensity measurement. Per-cell ROS generation was quantified as the ratio of ROS channel integrated density (IntDen) to nuclear channel IntDen, establishing a normalized metric for robust intergroup comparative analysis; this protocol was systematically applied to all subsequent analogous experiments to ensure methodological consistency.

Calcein-AM/PI staining
B16F10 cells (2×105 cells/mL) were seeded and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Then the cells were incubated with FP for 72 h and FIS for 4 h, respectively. Then, the cells were irradiated (808 nm, 1.0 W/cm2, 20 s) and stained by Calcein-AM (2.0 µM) and PI (4.5 µM) for 20 min, and then observed by CLSM (STELLARIS 8 STED, Leica, Germany), respectively. Viability quantification was performed using the dead/live cell ratio derived from PI channel IntDen normalized to calcein channel IntDen.

3D B16F10 tumor spheroid model for penetration
A three-dimensional cell spheroid model was established using a 96-well plate. 20 g/L agarose dissolved at 80 °C was added to each well, and 3×103 B16F10 cells were inoculated and cultured until the diameter of the cell spheroid was about 100 µm. The cell spheroids were treated with FP for 72 h and FIS for 4 h, then gently rinsed with PBS and fixed with 4% (m/v) paraformaldehyde. Finally, the cell spheroids were scanned layer by layer along the Z-axis to observe the penetration of tumor cell spheroids at different depths using CLSM (TCS SP8 STED, Leica, Germany). IR780 distribution was subsequently quantified by measuring layer-specific mean fluorescence intensity across all optical sections in ImageJ.

B16F10 solid tumor penetration in vivo
B16F10 cells were inoculated into the right flank of C57BL/6J mouse at 1×106 cells each. On the 10th day, tumor volume reached about 200–300 mm3. Mice were randomly divided into 2 groups: FIS and MAD, with one mouse per group for the representative experiment presented. After FP (10 µg plasmid for 20 g mice) was given peritumorally for 72 h and FIS (12 µg IR780 for 20 g mice) was given for 4 h, the tumor was removed and fixed with tissue fixative. After dehydration with 30% sucrose, the tumor was embedded in OCT embedding medium. Then the tumor tissue was sliced into frozen sections using a freezing microtome (Leica CM3050S, Germany), stained with WGA and Hoechst 33342, and observed with CLSM (STELLARIS 8 STED, Leica, Germany).

Anti-cancer therapy in mice bearing B16F10 solid tumor
B16F10 cells were inoculated into the right flank of C57BL/6J mouse at 1×106 cells each. On the 8th day, tumor volume reached about 100 mm3. Mice were randomly divided into 6 groups: ① Control (n=6), ② FP (n=6), ③ FIS+NIR(+) (n=6), ④ MAD+NIR(+) (n=6), ⑤ FIS+NIR(++) (n=7) and ⑥ MAD+NIR(++) (n=7). Animals were treated peritumorally according to schedule. NIR was irradiated with 808 nm laser at 1.0 W/cm2 for 5 min. Tumors were measured every other day using a vernier caliper, and tumor volume (mm3) was calculated as (long diameter × short diameter2)/2. Total body weight was routinely measured as a measure of any gross toxicity. When the tumor volume exceeded 2000 mm3, body weight loss surpassed 15% of the initial weight, or any other signs of distress were observed, mice were euthanized by cervical dislocation under anesthesia in accordance with the protocols approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Peking University Health Science Center.

When the tumor grew to the 12th day, two mice in each of groups ① and ② were euthanized and the tumors were isolated for western blot experiments; on the 19th day, mice in groups ①, ②, ③ and ④ were euthanized as shown in Supplementary Fig. S17 for H&E staining, Ki67 staining, western blot, immunofluorescence, flow cytometry and blood routine analysis; on the 26th day, the remaining mice in groups ①, ②, ③ and ④ were euthanized for western blot experiments; the survival of mice in groups ⑤ and ⑥ were observed until 60 days. Immunofluorescence data were quantified by normalizing target protein IntDen to nuclear channel IntDen. Western blot expression levels were calculated as target protein band intensity relative to loading control (GAPDH) band intensity, with both analyses performed using ImageJ.

Hematoxylin-eosin, Ki67, and immunofluorescence staining
Tumor tissues and major organs were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde and prepared into paraffin sections and frozen sections for immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence analysis, respectively. Immunohistochemistry was performed for H&E and Ki67 staining. Immunofluorescence was used for TUNEL assay and the detection of protein expression. All frozen sections were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100, blocked with 2% BSA, and incubated with primary antibody at 4 °C overnight. After washing with PBS, secondary antibody (AF488) was added for 1 h and DAPI was added for 5 min at RT. H&E and Ki67 images were taken using a digital pathology slide scanner (NanoZoomer, Hamamatsu, Japan). Immunofluorescence results were observed using CLSM (STELLARIS 8 STED, Leica, Germany). Quantitative analysis involved normalization of target protein IntDen to nuclear IntDen in ImageJ.

Statistical analysis
The data were expressed as the mean or mean ± standard deviation (SD). SPSS (IBM SPSS Statistics Version 26) and GraphPad Prism 8 were used for statistical analysis. Comparison between two groups was analyzed by two-tailed unpaired t test. Comparisons among multiple groups were analyzed by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s/Dunnett’s multiple comparisons test, two-way ANOVA with Sidak’s multiple comparisons test, or repeated-measure ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple comparisons test. P<0.05 was set as a significant difference. All experiments were repeated independently with similar results for the reproducibility of the results.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript submitted by Peng et al. concerns the inter-cellular transfer of mitochondria through tunnelling nano-tubes (TNTs), and their application as anti-cancer agents. The mitochondrial transfer field, particularly via TNTs, is an emerging field in cell biology, which has brought about a number of high profile publications relating to their properties, function and exploitation. In spite, of this many questions remain. Therefore, new finding of this hot topic will be very welcome to the TNT and wider mitochondrial community, and thus of interest to the broad readership of Nature Communications.
The paper is very interesting from 2 perspectives. First of all, it provides evidence for a link between mitophagy and TNT conducted mitochondrial transfer. Secondly, the work describes how TNTs could be deployed for the formation of extra-cellular networks for the delivery, and deep penetration, of agents for the purposes of imaging and therapy, such as tumor clearance. These two aspects are both very worthy topics in themselves, but feel very much like two different stories, which might be better suited as different papers. The two parts present very interesting fundamental new knowledge and novel applications, which could in principle be suitable for Nature Communications. However, before publication, either as one paper or two, there are a many concerns that need to be addressed.
A major concern is that the central feature of the paper – inter-cellular mitochondrial transport – has not been irrefutably demonstrated. We really need to see images/ movies of mitochondrial moving fully from one cell to another one. This also goes for other claims, e.g. that mitochondria can move in both directions, and reagents are able to hitch a ride on mitochondria from one cell to another; we need to see this happening. Given the claim of large scale inter-cellular mitochondrial traffic through TNTs this should be achievable.
Other concerns figure-by-figure:
Figure 1
A) Representative panels clearly present very different cell densities. It looks like the TNTs have been quantified by area, with each area containing a different number of cells. So, it might be misleading to state that TNTs are upregulated by siPINK1 treatment. Quantification of N=4 random regions is not really sufficient. Surely, the number of TNTs needs to be quantified per cell over a large number of cells from a suitable number of independent experiments. Furthermore, the assertion in the text that the TNTs span ‘from one cell to another’ is not clear from the images (related to major concern above).
B) In the co-culture it is not clear how the team avoided cross contamination of dyes and siRNAs. Can we be certain the co-localisation is not the result of residual dye/ siRNA carrying over from the cells used to seed the co-culture?
C) The combined red/ green channels make it hard to see red mitochondria within green cell. It would be much better to also show the 2 channels separately.
D) The Y-axis need clarification. What does ‘mitochondrial signalling/ cell area’ mean? The text states that there is an increase in the number of mitochondria and TNTs. The stated increase in mitochondria appears to be on the basis of an increase in mito-tracker intensity, which is not a reasonable assertion. The increase in TNTs needs to be properly quantified (as noted above).
Related to this section of the results we need to see some evidence that PINK1 is knocked down by the siRNA treatment (e.g. by Western blotting).
Figure 2
C) Why is the ‘knock out’ only 30% reduced in PINK1? Shouldn’t it be 100%.
E) Again, quantification is based on random regions of cells, rather than according to the number of cells. What does intensity density mean?
K) Has the Seahorse data been normalised to cell density/ number?
Figure 3
C) Please clarify – have the mitochondria in multiple cells of each type been properly quantified – i.e. more than 1 cell per condition from sufficient biological repeats?
F) Transfer in both directions must be shown (visualised) to claim bidirectionality; see major concern above.

Figure 4
C) Again – Y-axis needs clarification – what does mitochondrial signalling/ cell area mean, and what property does it relate to?
J) What was the purpose of Hoechst in this experiment?
Figure 5
A) Again – quantification is based on random regions of the slide, rather than the number of cells. Comparing A) versus B) – why do the same conditions looks completely different? In summary, the claim that all of the interesting effects onserved are mediated by inter-cellular mitochondrial and reagent transfer through TNT networks needs to be proven by visualisation and robust quantification.

### Reviewer 2

In this work, the authors constructed the ‘mitochondrial autonomous drive’ (MAD) system, which utilized the down-regulation of mitochondrial autophagy to accelerate mitochondrial intercellular transport and achieve the transportation of exogenous substances for photodynamic therapy of tumors. This provided a new strategy for non-transmembrane drug delivery. The work innovatively utilized mitochondria as drug carriers and achieved deep penetration and delivery of drugs through the tunneling nanotubes (TNTs). Moreover, it was the first to conduct a detailed study on the relationship between mitochondrial autophagy and intercellular transport, and found that inhibiting mitochondrial autophagy could significantly enhance the transport capacity of mitochondria. Overall, this is a well-prepared manuscript. However, there are still several shortcomings. I recommend the acceptance of this work after addressing the following issues.
Major issues:
1. In Fig 2k，FP treatment to knockout PINK1 can enhance the mitochondrial OXPHOS pathway that support the cell-to-cell transfer of mitochondria. Will the increased oxygen consuming lead to tumor hypoxia after FP treatment that limited the photodynamic effect? For this question, experiments that determine tumor oxygen condition is suggested.
2. In Fig 7b, it is intriguing that FP treatment inhibits tumor growth. The authors believe that knocking out PINK1 may increase oxidative stress that works for tumor inhibition. However, in Fig 5b, c, FP treatment shows negligible effects in killing tumor cells or generating ROS. Additional experiments are suggested to address this discrepancy.
3. Tumor tissues consist of various cell types, including immune cells and fibroblasts. Do FP or MAD treatments promote mitochondrial transport between these cells, potentially altering the tumor microenvironment? A recent study (doi: 10.1038/s41586-024-08439-0) reports that mitochondrial transfer from cancer cells to tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes can lead to immune evasion. To address potential concerns that MAD might facilitate tumor immune evasion, additional experiments are needed.
4. The mechanism of mitochondrial autophagy and intercellular transport is very complex. Although the article revealed some mechanisms, many details still need further research. For example, how the inhibition of mitochondrial autophagy specifically affects the formation and function of TNTs still needs in-depth exploration.
5. Further research is needed to study the long-term impact of inhibiting mitochondrial autophagy on cells and the body, as well as the stability and effectiveness of the MAD system in the complex physiological environment of the living body.
6. The article only used the photosensitizer IR780 as a model drug. Whether other types of drugs can also be effectively delivered through this system still needs to be verified. Moreover, there is a lack of comparison with other delivery systems to highlight the advantages of the MAD system in anti-tumor in this study.
Minor issues:
1. It is suggested to add a description of Fig 7a for the schematic illustration.
2. Please check the grammar usage and the format issues in the title and the manuscript. For example, in the title, “for accelerate transport” is suggested to change to “for accelerating transport”.

### Reviewer 4

Here the authors explore the relationship between mitophagy and mitochondrial transport between cells via tunnel nanotubes (TNTs) as a potential avenue for enhancing drug delivery. Mitochondria exhibit complex inter-and-intracellular dynamics, and the authors propose using them as a vector for delivering exogenous treatments. They find that inhibiting mitophagy increases transport of mitochondria (both in number and speed) between cells via TNTs. The authors use the photosensitive drug IR780 to develop a ‘mitochondrial autonomous drive’ system that enhances traffic of mitochondria deeper into tumor tissues to lead to improved outcomes in vitro and in vivo.
My expertise is in advanced light microscopy, so most of my comments concern imaging methodology and interpretation. The cell biology and therapeutic application here seem sound and exciting to me, but there are some flaws in the imaging methodology that need to be corrected for me to have full confidence in the conclusions of those experiments.
The biggest concern for me here is that many of the confocal images included in this analysis are saturated. Saturated images (images with pixel values of 255, in an 8-bit image) are incompatible with quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements. Saturation destroys the mostly-linear relationship between fluorophore density in a specimen and grey values in a digital image. Even a few saturated pixels in a region of interest will disrupt the linearity of the measurement and thus the integrity of the data. There are several instances in this study where saturated images are used for intensity measurements:
Fig 4e. The mitochondria and IR780 channels. In addition to breaking the linearity of intensity measurements, saturation can also cause erroneous dilation of objects and so can confound object-based colocalization analyses as well.
Fig 5b. All of the PI images in the MAD + NIR condition are extremely saturated.
Fig 5c. The DCFHDA images in the MAD + NIR condition
Fig S11. The brightest patches in most of the images are saturated. Pearson’s Correlation is particularly sensitive to saturation because it is impossible to accurately measure how two signals vary relative to one another if one or both of them have hit an upper limit.
I believe that to have full confidence in their image analysis results, the authors will need to re-image the saturated data using appropriate acquisition parameters. Chances are good that most of the major conclusions from these experiments will remain the same (for instance, in Fig 5b and c, saturation may even be causing an underestimation of how much more PI and DCFHDA there is in the MAD + NIR condition relative to the others), but in my experience as a microscopist it is not valid to make quantitative, absolute intensity measurements on saturated data. This is particularly true for sensitive analyses like colocalization and ratiometry.
Additionally bleedthrough controls should be included for most of not all multi-color imaging experiments. A notable example is Fig 4a. One of the conclusions of the figure is that IR780 traffics with mitochondria (labeled with MitoTracker), but signal from the MitoTracker channel bleeding into the IR780 channel would create the appearance of coincidence between the two signals. The authors don’t state which MitoTracker is used in this experiment, but if is MitoTracker Deep Red then bleedthrough is a definite possibility given that there is some overlap between the excitation spectra of MTDR (via FPbase.org) and IR780 (via Fig S9).
An autofluorescence control should be included to demonstrate that mitochondrial/cellular autofluorescence does not change when mitophagy is altered.
The rest of my comments are only minor points.
The image processing and analysis could use a bit more fleshing out, perhaps in the supplementary materials. “ND Processing” is a suite of analysis tools that is exclusive to NIS Elements, and so is not very informative to people who use other types of instruments. Indicating only that analysis was done in ImageJ, LAS, or Zen is not enough information to help people understand how the data was analyzed. How were images pre-processed? (background subtraction, etc)How were ROIs selected? (thresholding? If so, how?) How was particle tracking done?
Avoid displaying images in blue if possible – it is very difficult to see dark blue on a black background.
Overall, the findings here are exciting and significant as a potential avenue for drug delivery, but in my opinion some of the imaging needs to be redone without saturation in order to be analyzed appropriately, and bleedthrough controls should be included in the supplementary material where relevant.

Re: Your comments profoundly address a pivotal aspect central to our research
objectives, and we acknowledge that existing literature has provided foundational
insights into related mechanisms. To comprehensively explore this, we first consider
the multifaceted consequences of mitophagy inhibition—including the elevated
intracellular ROS levels, disruption of cellular energy homeostasis, accumulation of
dysfunctional mitochondria, amplified pro-inflammatory signaling through mtDNA

tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) demonstrate defining characteristics: their cytoskeleton-
dependent (primarily actin-based) dynamic assembly is regulated by diverse cues such
as cellular stress, damage signals, and specific receptor-ligand interactions.
Functionally, TNTs serve as critical conduits for intercellular communication,
transporting an extensive array of cargo spanning ions, signaling molecules, organelles
(notably mitochondria), pathogens, and prion-like aggregates. These structures play
indispensable roles in tissue homeostasis, immune responses, disease pathogenesis, and
neuronal signaling, with mitochondria representing a particularly consequential cargo
frequently trafficked through TNT networks.
Consequently, it is analytically evident that mitophagy inhibition may
significantly promote tunneling nanotube (TNT) formation, constituting a fundamental
cellular adaptive response to accumulated mitochondria and associated stress signaling.
First, amplified cellular stress signals serve as potent TNT inducers, as extensive studies
25
demonstrate that oxidative stress4, DNA damage5, and viral infections6 robustly
stimulate TNT biogenesis. Second, the mitochondrial crisis potentially triggers 'distress
signaling' wherein compromised cells initiate TNT formation as physical conduits to
solicit healthy mitochondria (mitochondrial donation) or restorative factors from
neighboring cells7. Third, although not yet addressed in our current manuscript, the pro-
inflammatory milieu resulting from mitophagy suppression (e.g., mtDNA leakage
activating the cGAS-STING pathway) further amplifies TNT generation8, particularly
in immune cell communication contexts.
These mechanistic insights align with our described findings, as we discussed in

as a possible link from inhibited mitophagy to TNT formation/mitochondrial transfer.
Functionally, inhibiting mitophagy profoundly alters the role of tunneling
nanotubes (TNTs), transforming them from potential rescue conduits into pathways that
propagate mitochondrial and cellular stress. This subverts TNTs' beneficial role in
maintaining intercellular mitochondrial quality homeostasis within tumors. In cancer
contexts—where hypoxic and metabolically stressed microenvironments prevail—
mitophagy suppression may promote the intercellular exchange of damaged
mitochondria through TNTs. While this could represent a survival strategy for cancer
cells under duress (e.g., disposing dysfunctional components to neighbors or
26
distributing cellular damage), it may simultaneously disseminate pro-apoptotic signals.
Notably, when leveraged for therapeutic cargo transport, this reprogrammed pathway
can be co-opted as a 'Trojan horse' for targeted drug delivery.
Although distinct, the driving forces for mitochondrial transfer highlighted in our
study (morphological adaptation, metabolic reprogramming, and respiratory
enhancement) largely overlap with those underlying TNT formation. The fundamental
premise is that when cells fail to recycle damaged mitochondria through mitophagy,
expelling these organelles may serve as a compensatory mechanism to prevent their
accumulation—with TNTs acting as the primary conduit for mitochondrial transfer.
In summary, current theoretical frameworks support that mitophagy inhibition
promotes tunneling nanotube (TNT) formation and mitochondrial transfer. Within our
experimental design, suppressing mitophagy serves additional strategic purposes: (1)
increasing mitochondrial availability for cargo loading, (2) preventing degradation of
mitochondrial transport machinery (e.g., Miro19), and (3) ensuring spatial concordance
between photosensitizer targeting and ROS generation at subcellular compartments.
